title: Permission Models for Autonomous Systems
summary: Reach and initiative are different questions. A table separating safe from idempotent from reversible, what MCP's tool annotations do and don't let you enforce, and how a checkpoint became a protocol message.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**Whether an agent can reach a system and how much initiative it gets once it is there are two different questions, and most permission models only ever answer the first one.**


The protocols have started answering the second. MCP's tool annotations carry` readOnlyHint` ,` destructiveHint` ,` idempotentHint` and` openWorldHint` , and the defaults are pessimistic on purpose:` destructiveHint` and` openWorldHint` both default to` true` . An unannotated tool is, by the spec's own defaults, destructive and open-world.


The common fix is a checkpoint on everything, and it fails for a reason the EU AI Act names in Article 14(4)(b): people asked to confirm hundreds of actions develop a "tendency of automatically relying or over-relying on the output", which is a signature you cannot audit your way out of.


We are not arguing that annotations solve this. The same spec says those properties are "hints" that are "not guaranteed to provide a faithful description of tool behavior", and clients MUST treat them as untrusted from untrusted servers. They sort your catalog. They cannot be your authorization input.


Sort every action an agent can attempt by what happens if it is wrong, using reversibility rather than which system it touches, and enforce the resulting tier where the call leaves your infrastructure.
